title: The page
hook: Mishnah and Gemara in the center, Rashi on the inner margin, Tosafot on the outer

segments.voice: Yesterday, aggadah, and your line: story and law together. Rabbi Yose's dove-voice, sitting in the middle of a legal page. This week you learned the sugya, the open question, light and heavy, the same word, Hillel's rules. Today, the page that holds them all. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

Hold a printed page of Talmud at arm's length, and before you read a single word, you see a shape. A block of large letters in the middle. Columns of smaller print wrapping around it on both sides, like hands cupping something. Notes squeezed into the edges. It looks less like a page of a book and more like a map of a city, with a town square in the center and streets leading out. That shape isn't decoration. Every block on it is somebody talking. Today, how to read the shape.
screen: `A BLOCK IN THE MIDDLE.` → `COLUMNS LIKE CUPPED HANDS.` → `A MAP OF A CITY.`

segments.voice: The page. In the standard printed Talmud, the pages share one basic layout, and once you know it, you can find your way around a tractate. First, the center. That large block holds the Mishnah and the Gemara: the case, then the voices, then the long conversation we've spent this week inside. It's the town square. Everything else on the page points back to it. Second, the inner margin, the column nearest the binding. That's Rashi, the explainer, walking alongside the text word by word, telling you what a phrase means and how the argument moves. If you're lost, you look to the inside. Third, the outer margin, the column nearest the edge. That's Tosafot, a circle of later scholars who ask hard questions: of the Gemara, of other pages, and sometimes of Rashi himself. So on a single page, the explainer and his questioners sit on either side of the text, facing each other across it. Fourth, the edges. Around and below, in still smaller print, are notes that send you elsewhere: to a verse, to a law code, to a parallel discussion on another page. One more thing. These voices lived in different places and different times, and none of them could hear the others in life. The printed page puts them within arm's reach of each other. A student who opens it steps into the middle. The page is a conversation.
screen: `THE CENTER: MISHNAH AND GEMARA.` · `INNER MARGIN: RASHI EXPLAINS.` · `OUTER MARGIN: TOSAFOT ASK.` · `THE EDGES SEND YOU ELSEWHERE.` · then, large: `THE PAGE IS A CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at a Talmud page. If you can, find a picture of one later; any page will do. For now, sit, close your eyes, and build it. The block in the center. Rashi on the inside, near the spine. Tosafot on the outside, near the edge. Little notes along the borders. Now put yourself on the page. Where would your voice go? Asking, explaining, sending someone elsewhere? Breathe there for a while, a small voice in a very old margin. The bell holds the time.
The page. Mishnah and Gemara in the center, Rashi on the inner margin, Tosafot on the outer, notes at the edges: one page, many voices. Today's word.

Your line: the page is a conversation. Today, notice one place where many voices share a single surface, a family fridge, a group chat, a shared document, and read it like a Talmud page. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Students of the Talmud learn the page's layout early: they read the Mishnah and Gemara in the center, turn to Rashi on the inner margin for explanation, and to Tosafot on the outer margin for questions and cross-references.

myth: Rashi's commentary sits on the outer margin of the page
Rashi is on the inner margin, nearest the binding; Tosafot is on the outer.
the explainer and his questioners sit on either side of the text, facing each other.
the voices on one page all lived and talked together
they lived in different places and times; the printed page brings them together.

fork.setup: you've opened a page of Talmud. there's an Aramaic phrase in the center block you can't make sense of. where do you look first?
options: the notes at the bottom edge.
fork.reveal: the inner margin, nearest the binding: that's Rashi, explaining the text word by word. the outer margin is where Tosafot ask their questions.

original.note: Hebrew: daf, the word learners use for a page of Talmud.

trapdoor: what you thought: a page of text with some footnotes.
what it means: a fixed layout: the text in the center, Rashi inside, Tosafot outside, notes at the edges.
what a scholar hears: the printed Talmud page as a designed conversation across centuries, with the explainer and his questioners facing each other across the Gemara.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, standard printed page layout (e.g. Berakhot 2a)

notes: Week-end day (days 1093–1099): the review looks back at the week.
Layout claims (center, inner margin Rashi, outer margin Tosafot, cross-reference notes at the edges) follow the index line; no century or edition is named, since day 1102 teaches the Vilna edition.

'The pages share one basic layout' is a generalization about the standard printed Talmud; on some pages (e.g. tractates where Rashi's commentary is not by Rashi, or the opening pages) the margins differ. Please confirm or soften.
'Different places and different centuries' is a general statement without naming dates, by design.
The original game teaches daf (page of Talmud) rather than the title; please confirm the word and pronunciation.

Editor: cut 'the great explainer', 'any tractate' and the stock 'here's the remarkable part'; 'centuries' softened to 'times'; replaced the 'one table' image, which day 1092 already used for the Gemara's sages, with 'within arm's reach' and 'a very old margin'.
